lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- Who Is Caio, in English?

lesson.grammar_point: third-person singular -s in the present simple

listenings.text: Okay, note to the team, end of day two. I met eleven founders today and I am going to be honest with you about something. The ones who lost me were not the ones with the worst English. Not even close. I am listening for three things and only three things. How big the company actually is. Where the money comes from, and whether it comes from one client or forty. And what the founder wants, in a sentence, without me having to ask twice. That is it. When somebody gives me all three in the first two minutes, everything after that is easier. And when a founder goes quiet on me, I write one word in the margin, and that word is almost never about English. It is about whether this person is going to tell me the difficult thing later, when it matters.

I have sat on both sides of maybe sixty cross-border deals, and I will tell you what goes in the report and what actually happened. The report says valuation. Valuation is the polite reason. The real reason, more often than anybody writes down, is that the buyer stopped believing the founder could run that company in their language. It happens in a very specific way. The founder loses the thread in one meeting, and instead of stopping the room, he lets it go. So the buyer starts directing questions to the chief financial officer instead. And from that moment on, the founder is not a partner in the deal. He is a risk on a slide. So here is my advice, and it is not about grammar. Learn to say the three sentences about your own company before you learn anything else. And never, ever let a meeting move forward on something you did not understand.

There is a finding in the exit data that keeps coming up, and nobody in the industry likes talking about it very much. Founders who negotiated their own exit in English closed at a higher multiple than founders who worked through an interpreter, and the businesses were the same size, in the same sectors, in the same years. The researchers went looking for the difference and it was not grammar. It was not accent either, which surprised almost everyone. What the successful group had in common was a single habit. They stopped the meeting the moment they lost the thread. They asked for the sentence again, out loud, in front of everybody, and nobody in the room thought less of them for it. The founders who lost value were the ones who nodded and hoped the next sentence would explain the last one.

extra_audio.text: Caio Amante. I am the founder and CEO of Dataside. We specialize in data and artificial intelligence. Our people work inside the client company, so it is consulting, not software. We have almost three hundred people, and most of our revenue comes from long contracts. Right now I am looking at expansion into the United States. And you, what does your firm look for in a company like ours?
